analysis.one_liner: Forgives portions of new federal student loans for public-service workers over ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in June 2017 with 10 Democratic cosponsors, it sat in the Senate's education committee until that Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the existing Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, a borrower's federal student loan balance is canceled only after 120 monthly payments made while working a qualifying public-service job. This bill would change that for loans taken out after its enactment: the government would cancel 15% of the balance after 2 years of public-service work, another 15% after 4, 20% after 6, 20% after 8, and the final 30% after 10 years. Borrowers would have to submit a form documenting their employment, their loans would be put on hold (deferment) while they worked the qualifying job, and any interest accrued in a year when part of the loan is forgiven would also be wiped out.
analysis.who_benefits: Teachers, nurses, social workers, law enforcement officers, military members, and other public-service employees who take out new federal student loans after the bill becomes law. Instead of waiting ten years and making 120 payments before any relief, they would see chunks of their balance canceled every two years, would not have to make payments on the loan while working the qualifying job, and would not be charged interest in years when part of the loan is forgiven.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public servants with new federal loans

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Education Department to cancel 15%, 15%, 20%, 20%, and 30% of the amount owed after 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 years of public-service employment respectively, instead of waiting for a single forgiveness after 120 payments.

Once a borrower submits an employment certification form — self-certification plus employer confirmation of employment dates — the loan goes into deferment, meaning no payments are due while the borrower works the qualifying job.
In any year when a portion of the loan is canceled, all interest that accrued on the loan for that year is canceled too, so the balance cannot quietly grow.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the Education Department's loan program. Every dollar of principal and interest forgiven is a dollar the government does not collect, and under this bill the government would start canceling balances as early as year two instead of waiting ten years.

drawbacks.text: The gradual forgiveness applies only to loans made after the bill's enactment, so it does nothing for current borrowers — including those already working public-service jobs under the existing program.

The schedule adds up to 100% forgiveness over ten years plus cancellation of accrued interest each year, meaning the federal government would forgo more money, earlier, than under the current pay-for-ten-years-then-forgive structure — a real cost to taxpayers.
The benefit is tied to having federal student debt and holding a qualifying job, so students who avoided debt, attended college and never borrowed, or left public service early get nothing from it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: public-service workers get meaningful, earlier debt relief in exchange for a larger and earlier cost to the federal loan program. The biggest design weakness is that it helps only future loans, leaving current borrowers — the group most frustrated with the existing program — without relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's education committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on June 22, 2017, joined by ten Democratic cosponsors including Senators Warren, Markey, Franken, Shaheen, Udall, Hirono, Hassan, and Feinstein.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal loan program was spared the cost of the earlier and larger forgiveness, and the status quo — including the existing 120-payment forgiveness program — stayed in place. Public-service workers with student debt gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal loan program's status quo

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase in loan cancellation for public-service workers over ten years.

for.name: 10 of 47 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill the day it was introduced and never scheduled it for consideration; no hearing, markup, or vote occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All eleven Senate supporters — the sponsor and ten cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired education committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: Earlier cancellation, deferment, and wiped-out interest mean smaller balances in repayment and less interest collected over the life of loans, shrinking servicing and collection revenue. Borrowers' gain is the industry's modest loss.
Graduates who take public-service jobs would carry less debt on the loans this bill covers, which modestly lowers the effective cost of a degree for students headed into public service.
